item.title: Physics Colloquium - Descartes, Du Châtelet, d’Alembert: How Collisions Transformed Physics — Wed Nov 4, 3:30 PM — None
item.description: Here is a familiar story: up until the early 17th century, physics was a part of philosophy, and then the Scientific Revolution happened culminating in Newton's Principia of 1687. After that, physics was a separate discipline. This story has been told many times, and challenged in many ways, but a common thread persists in which we think of 18th century physics as having already separated from philosophy and as offering a stable period of "normal science" within the "Newtonian paradigm." In fact, the split took another century of struggle and development by philosophers and mathematicians. I will make this vivid by tracing the central role of collision theory. I will argue that collisions lie at the heart of the origins of modern physics, from the break with Aristotelian physics to the eventual separation of physics from philosophy in the late 18th century. With the rise and fall of collisions as central to physics, the goals, methods, and subject-matter of physics were all transformed

item.title: Healing Arts Chicago: Growing the Creative Care Workforce — Wed Nov 4, 6:00 PM — Rubenstein Arts Center
item.description:
Dr. Meida McNeal from Chicago Department of Culture and Special Events/DCASE and resident artist Leyda "Lady Sol" Garcia will share Healing Arts Chicago, a cross-sector effort to grow the arts and health workforce by embedding artists in Chicago's federally-qualiﬁed mental health clinics.
This is the third of a three-part public conversation series bringing together arts, humanities, medicine and healthcare professionals, artists, community leaders, and students from Duke and Durham to explore how creative practices can support healing, connection, and wellbeing. From national, state, and local efforts to prescribe arts engagement for wellbeing, to emerging policy platforms and workforce development, each event hosts two handpicked leaders from arts and health professions to share work and insights.
This series is moderated by Dr. Sarah Wilbur, dance-and-health practitioner and arts-labor researcher (Dance & Theater Studies).

item.title: Notes from the Sex Worker Left: Lumpen Theory — Book Conversation with Heather Berg — Thu Nov 5, 12:00 PM — None
item.description:
Drawing on interviews with sex workers as well as their political and creative writings, Berg's book approaches sex workers as theorists of work, family, the state, respectability, care, and everyday resistance. Centering the perspective of the lumpenproletariat, Notes from the Sex Worker Left asks what becomes visible when those most criminalized and excluded from respectable political life are understood as thinkers at the edge of radical political theory.
The event will feature comments by Kathi Weeks and Tania Rispoli, followed by a response from Heather Berg and open discussion.
Heather Berg is Associate Professor of Labor Studies and Gender Studies at UCLA and the author of Porn Work: Sex, Labor, and Late Capitalism. Notes from the Sex Worker Left: Lumpen Theory is forthcoming from Duke University Press in October 2026.
Register here: https://forms.gle/4wvwZe73ucz1y9kB9
Source: Duke University

item.description:
Abstract: This talk will explore the beginning stages of a project intended to answer the question: do higher numbers/rates of child maltreatment cases investigated by CPS for prenatal drug exposure, and/or higher numbers/rates of referrals of those cases to law enforcement, result in a "chilling" effect on prenatal care? I will also consider fetal personhood and pregnancy criminalization trends in the context of a larger pro-natalist, white supremacist, and gender essentialist project undertaken by federal and state governments.

item.title: Before the First Symptom: A Fireside Chat with Ronit Freeman — Thu Nov 5, 4:00 PM — Innovate Carolina Junction
item.description:
On Thursday, Nov. 5, from 4 to 5 p.m. at Innovate Carolina Junction in Chapel Hill, Carolina Chief Innovation Officer Tommy Sowers hosts a fireside chat with Ronit Freeman, the UNC associate professor leading IMPEDE, a consortium backed by up to $24.8 million from ARPA-H to detect and treat protein-misfolding diseases like Alzheimer’s and pulmonary fibrosis before symptoms appear. They’ll discuss how she assembled a 100-person, multi-university team and an industry partner in weeks, how AI and simulation are tackling “undruggable” proteins, her path toward a pulmonary fibrosis venture, and how Carolina’s innovation ecosystem moves discoveries toward patients. The event is aimed at faculty, researchers, students, entrepreneurs, industry partners and anyone curious about turning big ideas into real-world impact.
Source: UNC Chapel Hill

item.title: 🎤 Karaoke Night at The Tavern (Thursday Edition) 🍻 — Thu Nov 5, 9:00 PM
item.description:
Discover Durham Together Looking for an actually fun night out in Durham? This is one of those spots where the whole place just clicks.
Huge bar. Pool tables. Darts. A full karaoke stage. And a crowd that’s there to have a good time — whether you’re singing, cheering people on, or just hanging with friends over drinks.
The karaoke here is genuinely awesome because people actually get into it. You’ll hear everything from pop punk and country to throwback rap, emo classics, rock anthems, and songs everyone ends up singing together by the end of the night.
No pressure to perform. No “serious singer” vibe. Just good energy, great people, and one of the most entertaining nights you can have in Durham.
Come solo, bring friends, grab a drink, play some pool, put your name on the list, or just enjoy the show. Either way, you’ll probably leave with a sore voice and a few new friends. 🎶

item.title: Getting Proper about Prompting: An Introduction to Prompt Engineering for Social Science and Survey Research — Fri Nov 6, 1:00 PM
item.description: Take a glance through recent news or social media and you would be hard-pressed not to see mentions of chatbots and artificial intelligence (AI) methods aimed at generating text, images and other content. Recent work by Eloundou and colleagues (2023) explored the potential impact of these types of generative AI on labor markets, and survey research, specifically was among the top two most impacted industries. Professor Andrew Ng has been cited as saying “AI won’t replace human workers, but ‘people that use it will replace people that don’t.’” Much of the way researchers in the social sciences and survey research are incorporating AI into their workflow involves some type of prompting. Prompt Engineering approaches along with more nuanced fine tuning approaches are being used and refined to better incorporate more robust approaches for AI incorporation into the research process. item.description:
Roughly 73 million Baby Boomers are leaving the workforce, the largest retirement wave in US history. Age-related retirements alone accounted for 65% of the entire decline in US employment between 2000 and 2019.
With every departure, decades of judgment and "how we really do it here" know-how that was never written down. It usually leaves quietly, until a costly mistake or a missed call reveals the gap. This workshop closes that gap before it opens and turns your deepest expertise into a skill anyone in your organization can summon on demand. item.title: Getting Proper about Prompting: An Introduction to Prompt Engineering for Social Science and Survey Research — Thu Dec 3, 1:30 PM
item.description: Take a glance through recent news or social media and you would be hard-pressed not to see mentions of chatbots and artificial intelligence (AI) methods aimed at generating text, images and other content. Recent work by Eloundou and colleagues (2023) explored the potential impact of these types of generative AI on labor markets, and survey research, specifically was among the top two most impacted industries. Professor Andrew Ng has been cited as saying “AI won’t replace human workers, but ‘people that use it will replace people that don’t.’” Much of the way researchers in the social sciences and survey research are incorporating AI into their workflow involves some type of prompting. Prompt Engineering approaches along with more nuanced fine tuning approaches are being used and refined to better incorporate more robust approaches for AI incorporation into the research process. item.title: Introduction to Qualtrics — Tue Jan 26, 2:00 PM
item.description:
Qualtrics is a powerful browser-based web-survey tool. It is available to UNC Chapel Hill faculty, staff, and students, for UNC-related projects. Qualtrics allows users to build complex surveys, distribute them, and analyze the responses all from one place.
In this course, we will cover basic Qualtrics functions beginning with an overview of survey options and settings, followed by hands-on practice programming and distributing a survey and downloading results. We will program some of the most common question and response types, customize requirements and validation, and add display logic, skip logic, and basic branch logic in the “survey flow”. We will then create and upload a contact list and discuss advantages and disadvantages of distributing the survey with a single reusable link vs. the survey mailer. Finally, we will cover a basic overview of the Data & Analysis tab for viewing, editing, and exporting raw data into various formats including .csv, .tsv, .excel, and .spss. Ot

item.description:

The exhibition is a speculative, immersive world-building study that invites guests to explore (geo)locating self and home amid a rapidly and frequently changing post-pandemic “new” world.
